questions.question: Distinguish economic growth from development, explain the main indicators with their weaknesses, and evaluate the two models used to explain where development happens.
questions.expected_answer: Economic growth is an increase in an economy's output, measurable in money; development is improvement in the quality of people's lives — health, education, choice and dignity — so growth can occur without development reaching the majority. The economic indicators are GDP, the value of goods and services produced inside a country in a year, and GNI, the income of a country's people wherever earned, both usually taken per capita to allow comparison; their weakness is the weakness of averages — they say nothing about distribution, which the Gini coefficient measures on a scale from zero toward one, with South Africa's among the world's highest. Social indicators go where money cannot: life expectancy, infant mortality — the most sensitive single test of living conditions — literacy, and access to safe water and sanitation; the Human Development Index combines a long and healthy life, knowledge and a decent standard of living into a score between zero and one, showing that equal incomes can produce unequal development depending on policy. The core-periphery model explains the map of unevenness: cores like Gauteng accumulate investment, skills and services while peripheries such as the former homelands supply labour and raw materials and receive remittances — and the model repeats at global, national and city scales. Rostow's model proposes five stages from traditional society through preconditions, take-off and drive to maturity to high mass consumption; it supplies useful vocabulary but is fairly criticised for assuming all countries repeat the West's path, ignoring colonial history and late-starter disadvantage, and treating development as guaranteed.

questions.question: Explain how the terms of trade trap raw-material exporters, and argue both sides of the development aid debate to a balanced conclusion.
questions.expected_answer: The colonial trading pattern persists: peripheral countries export primary products — ores, crops, crude — and import manufactured goods. Primary prices are volatile and drift downward relative to manufactures, so the terms of trade — the ratio of export prices to import prices — move against raw exporters: the same tonnage of ore buys fewer machines each year, and wealth flows to whoever does the making. The escape is beneficiation and industrialisation — processing materials at home to capture value added, as South African policy urges and as East Asia's export-led climb demonstrated — while protectionism in rich countries, especially farm subsidies, further tilts the field. On aid: in favour, humanitarian aid saves lives in emergencies; development and technical aid build clinics, schools, dams and skills beyond the budget's reach, and campaigns such as vaccination and HIV treatment have transformed societies. Against: long-term aid can create dependency — free food undercutting local farmers destroys the production it should build — aid leaks to corruption, tied aid serves the donor's companies and policies first, and debt-financed aid became the debt trap of the 1980s and 1990s. The balanced conclusion: aid works when it is capacity-building, answers local priorities and is temporary in intent; but fair trade rules and investment do more for development than charity.

questions.question: Assess South Africa's energy mix — coal, nuclear, hydro and renewables — and explain how sustainability applies to energy management and to soil conservation.
questions.expected_answer: Over four-fifths of South Africa's electricity comes from coal burned in thermal stations standing on the Mpumalanga coalfields: pulverised coal heats water to steam that spins turbines and generators. Coal is cheap, local, job-rich and delivers reliable baseload, but it makes the country a heavy per-capita carbon emitter, pollutes the Highveld's air, consumes scarce water, scars the land and leaks acid mine drainage toward rivers. Nuclear power at Koeberg is low-carbon and steady but costly, slow to build and leaves long-lived waste; hydro is limited by weak rivers, partly imported from Cahora Bassa, with pumped-storage schemes like Drakensberg and Ingula serving as giant batteries rather than sources. Renewables exploit exceptional endowments — Northern Cape solar around Upington, including concentrated solar with molten-salt storage, and Eastern and Western Cape wind farms — driven by competitive bidding that made them cheaper than new coal; their intermittency demands storage, flexible backup and grid strengthening, and the coal communities require a just transition of retraining and inclusion. Sustainability — meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own — binds it together: in energy, government must steer policy, procurement, standards and the transition; business must generate and buy clean power and cut consumption; individuals contribute through efficiency, solar water heating and switching off, since the cheapest kilowatt-hour is the one never used. Applied to soil — effectively non-renewable, forming a few centimetres in centuries while erosion takes hundreds of millions of tonnes a year — sustainability means cover crops and residue, contour ploughing, terracing, rotation, stocking to carrying capacity, and gabions to heal dongas: living off the interest of natural systems, never the capital.
